# Platform differences

<!-- Generated by scripts/check_shared_contracts.py --write-report from
     scripts/ci/platform-differences.toml and scripts/ci/clone-baseline.toml. Do not edit by
     hand; the default check fails when this file is stale. -->

Every difference between products (Piers, Decks) must be **earned**: an
operating-system API or behaviour forces it. Anything else is a gap to
close or logic to move to `shared/`. This page is the ledger of both.

- **Earned differences** name the OS API or behaviour and cite the code.
- **Open gaps** are differences nobody has earned. Each has an owner; it
  closes when parity lands or when it is earned with evidence. "Not
  implemented yet" and "not possible" are different statements.
- `python3 scripts/check_shared_contracts.py` fails when an OS-conditional
  `cfg` in `shared/` has no row, a citation no longer holds, the
  capability matrix disagrees with the code, a new local copy of shared
  logic appears, a `platform` config key has no row, or cross-product
  clones grow past the baseline.

To add a difference, edit the ledger and run
`python3 scripts/check_shared_contracts.py --write-report`.

| PD-018 | file security | Windows Pier, macOS Deck, Windows Deck, `shared/deck-core`, `shared/observability` | Private-file checks and creation modes. | POSIX mode bits, owner and O_NOFOLLOW on Unix; security descriptors, owners and reparse points on Windows, where files inherit an ACL instead of taking a mode. A file without a name while open (a sealed support bundle's plaintext) is unlink-while-open on Unix and FILE_FLAG_DELETE_ON_CLOSE on Windows, which cannot unlink an open file; FILE_FLAG_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT opens a reparse point instead of following it. A support-bundle source path is walked folder by folder: on Unix with openat(O_NOFOLLOW) relative to the folder before (rustix), following only a link whose owner and folder (uid, mode bits) show nobody else could have made it, and opening the file O_NONBLOCK so a FIFO cannot block; Win32 has no open relative to a handle and no owner/mode facts for a reparse point, so every folder is opened by path with FILE_FLAG_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT, any reparse point is refused, and each handle's GetFinalPathNameByHandleW location must sit inside the one before. Identity is fstat device and inode on Unix; on Windows the 64-bit volume serial and 128-bit FILE_ID_128 from GetFileInformationByHandleEx(FileIdInfo) (the 64-bit index only where FileIdInfo is unsupported), with GetVolumeInformationByHandleW's FILE_SUPPORTS_OPEN_BY_FILE_ID and FileRemoteProtocolInfo saying whether the volume can prove it (std exposes none of these on stable). | PD-035 | pen barrel buttons | Linux Pier, Windows Pier, macOS Pier, Windows Deck, macOS Deck | Where a pen's barrel buttons come from and how they are clicked. The wire names what a button does (PenEventMsg.buttons: bit 0 right click, bit 1 middle; capability pen_button_actions) and the mapping, settings and legacy-host layout are shared (arcen_input::pen_buttons). Decks: Windows reads one barrel button (PEN_FLAG_BARREL) and its tablet driver's mouse clicks while the pen is in range, so its settings show one Pen button; macOS reads the lower and upper side switch by position (buttonMask) and its driver's right/other-mouse tablet events, so its settings show two. Piers: Linux presses BTN_STYLUS2 for the right click and BTN_STYLUS for the middle; Windows sets the Windows Ink barrel for the right click and sends a mouse middle click for the middle; macOS posts right/other mouse events with tablet data. | Windows Ink has one barrel switch (POINTER_PEN_INFO.penFlags PEN_FLAG_BARREL; an injected POINTER_FLAG_SECONDBUTTON is ignored for a synthetic pen), AppKit reports a pen's two side switches by position (NSEventButtonMaskPenLowerSide/UpperSide), and Linux desktops make BTN_STYLUS a middle and BTN_STYLUS2 a right click (xf86-input-libinput, xf86-input-wacom, GNOME/KDE stylus defaults). | `hosts/linux/src/input/pen.rs` (`BUTTON_STYLUS2_BIT`)<br>`hosts/windows/src/input.rs` (`pen_middle_click`)<br>`hosts/macos/src/input/mod.rs` (`barrel_button`)<br>`clients/windows/src/input/pen.rs` (`route_mouse_while_pen`)<br>`clients/macos/src/tablet/sample.rs` (`driver_click_for_event`) | `docs/architecture/pen-tablet-input.md` |
| PD-037 | TLS material | Linux Pier, Windows Pier, macOS Pier | What asks a running Pier to reload its TLS material: SIGHUP on Linux (systemctl reload arcen-pier) and macOS (launchctl kill HUP system/pier.arcen.tech.service), service control 202 on Windows (sc.exe control ArcenPier 202). The reload, its checks and its events are shared (HostTlsMaterial::reload, status_events). | A Windows service receives no POSIX signals; the Service Control Manager delivers user-defined control codes (128-255) to its handler instead. systemd and launchd deliver signals. | `hosts/linux/src/service_signals.rs` (`hangup`)<br>`hosts/macos/src/tls_material.rs` (`hangup`)<br>`hosts/windows/src/service.rs` (`SERVICE_CONTROL_RELOAD_TLS`)<br>`shared/transport/src/host_material.rs` (`fn reload`) | — |
| PD-038 | Native tablet route | Linux Pier, Windows Pier, macOS Pier | How a Pier brings a Deck's bridged tablet into the desktop. The route decision, the pen readers, the attachment, what a read pen claims and the Deck's wording are shared (arcen_usb_bridge::joined_pen::native_tablet_route, host_pen_bridge, arcen_input::bridged_pen). Linux publishes the tablet to its kernel through vhci-hcd for a dedicated Xorg desktop or a desktop on its own Arcen seat (the host driver route), and on a joined console reads the pen itself and posts it through its typed uinput pen (HidPublishPolicy::Nothing) once that device is proved to reach the joined X server alone. Windows always reads the pen itself (HidPublishPolicy::Nothing, Windows Ink). macOS reads the pen itself and publishes only pen and vendor interfaces (HidPublishPolicy::PenAndVendorOnly). | Linux has an in-tree virtual USB host controller (vhci-hcd) and per-device udev/Xorg routing, but a joined console's X server is not one Arcen starts, so a raw bridged device cannot be confined to it (it ignores the arcen_bridge tag and has no per-desktop class); its typed uinput device is offered to every reader on seat0, so its readers are proved from /proc and logind's seat record. Windows has no virtual USB host controller or HID device without a kernel driver (ADR 0017). An IOHIDUserDevice on macOS is system-wide (ADR 0022). | `hosts/linux/src/net/joined_pen.rs` (`HidPublishPolicy::Nothing`)<br>`hosts/linux/src/input/joined_devices.rs` (`listening_x_sockets`)<br>`hosts/linux/src/usb_bridge/mod.rs` (`attach_x11_desktop`)<br>`hosts/windows/src/session.rs` (`NATIVE_TABLET_POLICY`)<br>`hosts/macos/src/bridged_tablet.rs` (`PUBLISH_POLICY`) | `docs/architecture/pen-tablet-input.md` |

Routes for the window: detach before the sign-in opens the session, as LocalSystem on the console's input desktop (the technique console_recovery already uses for restore-display --console); for the refused desks: prefer an NVIDIA head with nothing physically connected in nvapi_headless provisioning when desk privacy is on, or a supported virtual display. Proved on the lab vGPU guest only (a head reporting itself physically connected detached and restored after the Deck left and after the session agent was killed); not on a physical workstation. The GeForce-plus-virtual-display case (a negotiated display, deskside::virtual_output_instead_of, DisplayLease::detach_desk_monitors) is covered by unit tests only, not on a real PC. | Windows Host | `hosts/windows/src/display.rs` (`detach_desk_monitors`)<br>`hosts/windows/src/deskside.rs` (`virtual_output_instead_of`)<br>`hosts/windows/src/deskside.rs` (`prove_desk_dark`)<br>`shared/session/src/console_session/desk_privacy.rs` (`desk_outputs_dark`) |

Low-level hooks do not see pointer (pen and touch) input on Windows; the routes considered are taking the desk's HID digitizers (disable or exclusive open while attached, re-enabled on detach and by the display watchdog's recovery) or a pointer-input redirection of the console session. Neither is built; the lab Windows Pier has no desk pen or touch screen to prove either on. The mouse hook's liveness is not proved by a canary either: on the lab vGPU guest Windows never calls WH_MOUSE_LL for an injected move (relative or absolute) while the keyboard hook on the same thread is called at once, so desk privacy's default proves the hook thread with the keyboard canary (InputHookGuard::install_keyboard_proved); blocking a physical desk mouse is unit-tested, not lab-proven. | Windows Host | `hosts/windows/src/deskside.rs` (`InputHookGuard`)<br>`hosts/windows/src/input.rs` (`InjectSyntheticPointerInput`) |

Unlike an X11 console it is not held for a resume (GNOME closes sharing on lock), a session shown on a monitor at the desk is refused while desk privacy is on (`desk_privacy`: a Wayland desk cannot be blanked without changing the compositor), and a Wayland login screen is still refused `console_wayland_session` (ADR 0025 section 9). | Not implemented yet. Done: S4a (the target and ownership contract), S4c-2 (no desktop beside an account's session), S4b (the join, proved on a task-owned GNOME 49 session without a display connector). Missing: desk privacy for physical monitors without changing the compositor; a remote-first sign-in through a Wayland login screen (GDM 47 has no third-party route; GDM 50 adds CreateUserDisplay); the resume hold across a lock; S4c, persistent per-user Wayland sessions; and native proof on a host with a display connector and GDM's login screen. | Linux Host | `shared/session/src/console_session/wayland_attach.rs` (`desk_privacy`)<br>`shared/session/src/console_session/wayland_attach.rs` (`AFTER_DECK_LEFT`)<br>`hosts/linux/src/session/wayland/join.rs` (`JoinedSession`) |

It would build the same shared ConsoleNotice. | Shared/Architecture | `shared/session/src/console_session/foreign_service.rs` (`ConsoleNotice`) |

capability's proof pattern, and a PD or GAP cell must not be.
